- sustainability is a major societal objective
- computational science and engineering is a major enabling technology
- but sustainability is rarely explicit in method-oriented CSE research

## Conclusions

- CSE papers optimize accuracy, runtime, scalability, and robustness
- but they rarely frame those choices as sustainability choices
- method-oriented work often looks detached from the sustainability discourse

Sustainable development goals are visible in application-facing projects.

Methodological CSE often contributes indirectly, but rarely names sustainability explicitly.

That mismatch motivates a second question.

If CSE helps design a more sustainable world, how sustainable is CSE itself?

# The idea of sustainability {.unnumbered}

## The idea of sustainability (Carlowitz)

We typically attribute the sustainability idea to **Hans Carl von Carlowitz**.

- early forestry formulation in *Sylvicultura oeconomica* (`1713`)
- manage forests such that harvest does not outrun regrowth
- famous because it turned forest use into an explicit long-term management problem

\tiny Carlowitz's *Sylvicultura oeconomica* (1713) is widely cited as an early forestry formulation of sustainability [@carlowitz_1713_biblio; @fao_sustainability_forestry].


## Deep dive: The challenge was economic pressure 

::: columns

::: {.column width="34%"}

Carlowitz was not primarily writing as a conservation activist.

He was a leading mining administrator in Saxony facing a real **decision-support problem**:

- reconstruction after the Thirty Years' War
- expanding mining and metallurgy
- rising timber prices and transport distances
- growing pressure on economically accessible wood

The core issue was operational:

How do we keep a resource-dependent system running when demand grows faster than renewal?

:::

::: {.column width="66%"}

```{=html}
<div style="width:100%; max-width:920px; margin:0 auto; border-radius:18px; overflow:hidden; box-shadow:0 18px 40px rgba(28,45,66,0.18); border:1px solid rgba(28,45,66,0.10); background:#f4f7fb; padding:10px;">
  <iframe
    data-external="1"
    src="origin_sustainability_plot.html"
    width="100%"
    height="590"
    style="display:block; border:none; background:#f4f7fb; border-radius:12px;"
    loading="lazy"></iframe>
</div>
```

:::

:::::


## The real systems insight

::: columns

::: {.column width="38%"}

The key difficulty was that the **scope of the decision** rested on a time-scale much shorter than the regeneration time of the system it controlled.

So sustainable management required reliable anticipation of the future, not only reactive correction.

Implications:

- sustainability is more than just green energy
- it is about balancing resource availability and demand as a dynamical system under shifting pressures
- it requires predictive decision support whenever resource response times exceed operational decision horizons

:::

::: {.column width="62%"}

```{=html}
<div style="width:100%; max-width:900px; margin:0 auto; border-radius:18px; overflow:hidden; box-shadow:0 18px 40px rgba(28,45,66,0.18); border:1px solid rgba(28,45,66,0.10); background:#f4f7fb; padding:10px;">
```

## It's not about indicators, it's about dynamics!

$T_regeneration$ >> $T_decision$


# Toward Sustainability in CSE

## The internal perspective

If CSE wants to contribute credibly to sustainability elsewhere, it must reflect on:

- its own energy footprint
- the longevity of its knowledge and software
- its future relevance as a field


## A simple framing for sustainable CSE

::: columns

::: {.column width="32%"}

**Sustainable computing**

- resource-aware models
- efficient algorithms
- energy-aware workflows

:::

::: {.column width="32%"}

**Sustainable software**

- reusable code
- reproducible results
- maintainable ecosystems

:::

::: {.column width="36%"}

**Stakeholder action**

- incentives
- infrastructure
- education

:::

::::

Sustainable CSE emerges when these three dimensions reinforce each other.


## Three sustainability aspects, and why they matter now

```{=html}
<div class="framework-two-col">
  <section class="framework-card">
    <h3>Three sustainability aspects within CSE</h3>
    <ol>
      <li>Energy footprint of computational work</li>
      <li>Longevity and reuse of CSE knowledge</li>
      <li>Future relevance of CSE in an AI-rich landscape</li>
    </ol>
  </section>
  <section class="framework-card">
    <h3>Why this matters now</h3>
    <ul>
      <li>workflows are becoming more complex</li>
      <li>software stacks are becoming more fragile</li>
      <li>AI-HPC pipelines increase both opportunity and waste</li>
      <li>scientific value is easily lost in irreproducible computation</li>
    </ul>
  </section>
</div>
```


## CSE bottlenecks are shifting

::: columns

::: {.column width="48%"}

**Traditional bottlenecks**

- compute access
- parallelization competence
- memory and storage
- raw implementation effort

:::

::: {.column width="52%"}

**Emerging bottlenecks**

- workflow complexity
- software fragility
- reproducibility gaps
- AI integration
- long-term maintainability

:::

::::


# Sustainable Computing

## Sustainable computing is about deliberate trade-offs

It asks how computational work should be designed so that scientific benefit, runtime, and resource use are balanced consciously.


## Sustainable computing means allocating effort where it matters

```{=html}
<div class="framework-two-col">
  <section class="framework-card">
    <h3>Three levers</h3>
    <ol>
      <li>Hardware efficiency</li>
      <li>Algorithmic efficiency</li>
      <li>Model efficiency</li>
    </ol>
  </section>
  <section class="framework-card">
    <h3>What that means in practice</h3>
    <ul>
      <li>invest degrees of freedom only where they matter</li>
      <li>connect accuracy targets to computational effort</li>
      <li>let quantities of interest drive computational investment</li>
      <li>spend extra effort only where it changes the answer materially</li>
    </ul>
  </section>
</div>
<div class="framework-center-line">Sustainable computing is not just about doing less. It is about spending effort where it produces meaningful scientific return.</div>
```


## Algorithmic differentiation and related levers

- gradients without fragile hand-derived code
- lower development burden in optimization workflows
- better maintainability and extensibility
- efficiency is computational and human


## Model hierarchies and multi-fidelity workflows

- cheap models for screening
- expensive models for verification and critical cases
- match fidelity to decision relevance


## Monitoring resource consumption

- measurement creates visibility
- visibility enables accountability
- accountability can shape better workflows


## Why ALUMET matters

- application-level energy attribution is hard on shared CPU/GPU systems
- runtime alone is often an unreliable proxy for energy consumption
- sustainable CSE needs measurement that reflects actual computational cost
- ALUMET helps close the gap between raw telemetry and actionable energy awareness


## ALUMET as enabler

- modular, lightweight framework for energy and system measurement
- plugin-based pipeline: gather, transform, export
- adaptable across heterogeneous hardware and workflow contexts
- enables downstream analysis and interpretation through tools such as Alumet-Insight
- turns energy awareness into something usable for research software and workflows


## Interim conclusion on sustainable computing

Sustainable computing is a workflow-level design principle.

It links models, algorithms, software, and infrastructure.


# Sustainable Software

## Software is the heart of CSE

- software carries methods into practice
- software preserves or loses knowledge
- software quality shapes the long-term impact of research


## Sustainable software means more than code availability

```{=html}
<div class="framework-two-col">
  <section class="framework-card">
    <h3>Properties of sustainable software</h3>
    <ul>
      <li>maintainability</li>
      <li>reproducibility</li>
      <li>accessibility</li>
      <li>extensibility</li>
      <li>portability</li>
      <li>community uptake</li>
    </ul>
  </section>
  <section class="framework-card">
    <h3>Two roles of software in CSE</h3>
    <ol>
      <li>Scientific application layer</li>
      <li>Enabling infrastructure layer</li>
    </ol>
  </section>
</div>
```


## Why software sustainability is scientific, not administrative

- it reduces duplication of effort
- it enables validation and extension
- it supports cross-institutional collaboration
- it preserves method knowledge beyond one project cycle


## Research software is part of the scholarly output

If software remains invisible in incentives and review, unsustainable practices are structurally reinforced.


# Recommendations and Structural Consequences

## Sustainable CSE needs structure, not only goodwill

```{=html}
<div class="framework-two-col">
  <section class="framework-card">
    <h3>Why individual goodwill is not enough</h3>
    <ul>
      <li>sustainable practice often has delayed returns</li>
      <li>short projects reward local optimization</li>
      <li>institutions shape what is feasible and visible</li>
    </ul>
  </section>
  <section class="framework-card">
    <h3>Stakeholders who shape sustainable CSE</h3>
    <ul>
      <li>funding agencies</li>
      <li>supercomputing centers</li>
      <li>research institutions</li>
      <li>journals and publishers</li>
      <li>industry and project leaders</li>
      <li>educators and young scientists</li>
    </ul>
  </section>
</div>
<div class="framework-center-line">Sustainable CSE requires sustainable computing, sustainable software, and coordinated institutional support.</div>
```


# Beyond the Manuscript

## My stronger claim today

The manuscript was necessary.

Sustainable CSE is not merely a topic area. It is a methodology.


## The core methodological question

Sustainable CSE asks:

How do we maximize trustworthy information return per computational investment?


## Computational investment and information return

```{=html}
<div class="framework-two-col">
  <section class="framework-card">
    <h3>Computational investment includes</h3>
    <ul>
      <li>compute time</li>
      <li>energy</li>
      <li>human development effort</li>
      <li>workflow complexity</li>
      <li>software maintenance</li>
      <li>data generation and curation</li>
    </ul>
  </section>
  <section class="framework-card">
    <h3>Information return includes</h3>
    <ul>
      <li>reduced uncertainty</li>
      <li>trustworthy predictions</li>
      <li>actionable design guidance</li>
      <li>transferable method knowledge</li>
      <li>reusable software and workflows</li>
    </ul>
  </section>
</div>
<div class="framework-center-line">The methodological task is to increase trustworthy information return per unit of computational investment.</div>
```


## This is already native to CSE

- error control already asks what accuracy is needed
- adaptivity already allocates resources selectively
- model hierarchies already trade cost against insight
- numerical analysis already disciplines approximation


## Sustainable CSE is principled approximation

The point is not to compute less at all costs.

The point is to compute as much as needed, for the right reason, at the right fidelity.


## AI makes this more urgent

- AI can amplify scientific productivity
- AI can also amplify waste, opacity, and fragility
- CSE has the tools to make AI workflows more principled


## My synthesis

Sustainable CSE is the disciplined pursuit of lasting scientific value from computational effort.


# Closing

## Final message

If CSE wants to remain a key enabling discipline, it must make sustainability explicit in how it designs methods, software, and workflows.
